input.rationale: Opened a sourced question about a public interface promise. ConfigurationStore documents StoreConfiguration as invoked once a log entry containing a configuration change is committed, and BatchingFSM documents that ApplyBatch receives LogConfiguration entries. runFSM chooses one path per FSM: applySingle calls StoreConfiguration for a configuration entry, and applyBatch never does, so an FSM that implements both interfaces should only ever see configuration changes through ApplyBatch. A construction run of the probe bears that out and is the reason the question is worth a retained execution: the ConfigurationStore-only FSM recorded the configuration change through StoreConfiguration, while the FSM implementing both recorded none and saw the same entries in ApplyBatch. The probe builds each case with the repository's own cluster helper, triggers one configuration change by moving an existing voter's address, and reports the callback counts. Execution is requested; the event values decide the question rather than this rationale.

investigations.question: When an application FSM implements both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore, is StoreConfiguration invoked for a committed configuration change as its documentation states, or is the change delivered only through ApplyBatch?
investigations.hypothesis: runFSM's applySingle calls StoreConfiguration for LogConfiguration entries only when the FSM is not a BatchingFSM, because applyBatch takes over entirely once batchingEnabled is true and handles configuration entries by sending them to ApplyBatch; the batching path contains no StoreConfiguration call, so the promise is not kept for an FSM that implements both interfaces.
investigations.discriminator: The callback counts of an FSM implementing both interfaces compared with an FSM implementing only ConfigurationStore, after one configuration change is committed through the leader.

scope.description: Two cases, each a three-voter cluster built with the repository's own cluster helper whose FSMs share a recorder: one case where the FSM implements FSM and ConfigurationStore, and one where it also implements BatchingFSM. Each case triggers a single configuration change by moving an existing voter's address, waits until the change reaches the FSM, and reports how many times StoreConfiguration and ApplyBatch were called with configuration entries.
assumptions: Moving an existing voter's address is a legal configuration change that nextConfiguration accepts for a voter, and with three voters the entry commits on the leader and one other node before the moved address matters.
The recorder is shared across the cluster's FSMs only to answer whether the callback is ever invoked anywhere in the cluster; per-node attribution is not needed for that question.
The cluster helper builds in-memory transports and stores, so no external service is involved.
excluded: Whether an application should rely on StoreConfiguration when it also batches, and any behaviour of ApplyBatch ordering or responses.

experiment.prefix: Each case calls MakeClusterCustom with three peers, bootstrapping and the in-memory test configuration, and a MakeFSMFunc that returns either an FSM implementing FSM and ConfigurationStore or one that also implements ApplyBatch; both record every callback into a shared recorder. The case emits assurance_config_store_setup, picks a follower, calls leader.AddVoter with that follower's ID and a new address (so that the configuration changes without removing anyone), waits up to five seconds for either callback counter to become non-zero, waits a further 200ms, and emits assurance_config_store_result with the call counts. The harness is TestAssuranceConfigurationStoreWithBatching.

comparisons.description: An FSM implementing both interfaces: whether the documented StoreConfiguration callback arrives for a committed configuration change.
The same case: whether the configuration entry was delivered through ApplyBatch instead.
Control: an FSM implementing only ConfigurationStore does receive the callback, so the difference is the batching interface and not the trigger.
Control: the non-batching FSM sees no ApplyBatch call at all.

investigations.question: When the leader of a cluster that includes a non-voter can reach only that non-voter, does VerifyLeader's success still establish the voter-majority contact its stale-read protection is meant to provide?
investigations.hypothesis: VerifyLeader returns nil in that partition because the non-voter's AppendEntries acknowledgement is counted as a vote toward a quorum sized only over voters: quorumSize() counts voters in the latest configuration, while verifyFuture.vote increments on any notifyAll(true) arriving from any replication peer. Without any reachable peer the same call does not succeed, so the acknowledging non-voter is what satisfies the quorum.
investigations.discriminator: The returned endpoint of VerifyLeader at a leader partitioned so that (a) only the non-voter is reachable, (b) one voter is reachable, and (c) no peer is reachable, together with the quorum size and the suffrage of each server in the leader's latest configuration.

gaps.question: Which legal condition, if any, lets a successor be elected while the old leader still reports VerifyLeader success, given that the leader lease counts voters only and ReloadConfig cannot raise LeaderLeaseTimeout above HeartbeatTimeout?

investigations.question: When LeadershipTransferToServer names a non-voter, does the call report a transfer that the named server can actually complete, and what happens to the cluster's leadership while it cannot?
investigations.hypothesis: The leader does not check that the requested target holds a vote. It resolves the target through leaderState.replState, which holds an entry for every configured server except the leader itself, so a non-voter passes that check and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow makes it a candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer set, which skips pre-vote by design, so it sends a real RequestVote with a higher term. Each voter adopts that higher term and steps down before reaching the hasVote rejection, then refuses the vote because the candidate has no vote, so no server grants the transfer, yet the leader's transfer goroutine reports success when it observes its own leadership loss. The prediction is that the call returns nil while the requested target never becomes leader, whereas the same call naming a voter does transfer leadership.
investigations.discriminator: The transfer future's reported result compared with the state of the requested target and of the cluster's leadership, in two cases that differ only in the target's suffrage in the leader's latest configuration.

gaps.question: After a transfer request naming a non-voter, how long is the cluster without a leader, and does the previous leader lose leadership and the higher term before a new election completes?

investigations.question: When a leader's main loop is stalled past its lease while a voter majority elects a successor, can a VerifyLeader request queued during the stall still report success by counting the reachable non-voter's acknowledgement?
investigations.hypothesis: During the stall the leader keeps Leader state and its replication goroutines keep running, so a successor can be elected while the old leader still believes itself leader. The queued VerifyLeader cannot be served while the main loop is blocked; once the stall ends both the lease case and the verify case are ready, so the verify either registers and is answered nil after the non-voter's acknowledgement arrives, or the lease case is served first and the request is answered with leadership loss.
investigations.discriminator: The VerifyLeader endpoint of each trial alongside whether a different server was observed in Leader state while the stalled leader was still Leader, and the terms those servers held.

investigations.question: Can a future returned by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown is in progress be left permanently uncompleted, so that the caller's Error() never returns?
investigations.hypothesis: Each call creates a future whose send races the shutdown channel in one select. The channels are buffered (64 for verifyCh), so the send is ready immediately; when Shutdown closes shutdownCh the run loop may take the shutdown case with futures still queued, and because none of these futures sets ShutdownCh, deferError.Error() has nothing to unblock on. VerifyLeader should be the most exposed because the leader loop drains verifyCh one case per iteration, while applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries per iteration and Barrier shares that path.
investigations.discriminator: The number of futures per API call kind that have not completed 400ms after Shutdown() has returned, compared with the same call kinds on a node that is not shut down.

investigations.question: Can a follower hold a committed configuration that was never committed and then truncate its log so that its latest configuration names a server with no configuration entry behind it, and what does it do with that configuration?
investigations.hypothesis: processConfigurationLogEntry advances the committed configuration to the previous latest configuration whenever it installs a new one, without checking that the previous one was actually committed, and the appendEntries truncation path resets the latest configuration to the committed one when the conflicting suffix reaches past latestIndex. If a follower appends a configuration entry the leader never commits and later truncates that entry away, its latest configuration can still name the servers from that entry.
investigations.discriminator: A trace or probe that appends a configuration entry at a follower, leaves the leader's commit index below it, then forces the follower to truncate that index and compares the follower's latest configuration with the entries actually present in its log, together with what the follower then uses that configuration for (vote granting, election participation, lease counting).

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits one CA_EVENT with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the quorum size, the leader term, the other servers' terms and states, the leader's state after the call, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport; the transports are fully connected before any node is started. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming all three as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, and the case waits until the leader's latest configuration reports the non-voter before proceeding. Configuration: HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, CommitTimeout = 5ms, default ProtocolVersion, which satisfies Config.Validate. After a 300ms settling period the transports are disconnected in both directions across the chosen boundary, so only the listed peers remain reachable from the leader; the observation then calls VerifyLeader() on the leader and reports nil, a concrete error, or pending after a 900ms wait. The peer kept reachable as a voter is chosen by position in the bootstrap configuration, and the non-voter by its join identity, never by a measured result.

experiments.revision_reason: The previous harness emitted CA_EVENT objects without an event name, so the controller rejected all three as invalid_observation and no observation could be interpreted. This revision only changes the observation format: each case now emits a named assurance_partition_setup event before the partition and a named assurance_verify_leader_result event afterwards, carrying the same measured fields, and declares the setup event as a prerequisite admission with one comparison per partition case.

scope.description: Observe what LeadershipTransferToServer reports against which server actually takes leadership when the requested target is a non-voter, with the same call naming a voter as the only difference. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event describing the leader, the chosen target, its suffrage in the leader's latest configuration and the voter set, then an assurance_transfer_result event with the returned result, the target's and old leader's states, the leader set and terms after the call, and the time until any leader is observed.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; protocol version is the default (>= 3), so LeadershipTransferToServer is supported.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a real transfer rather than a probe that never succeeds.
excluded: Bounding the length of any leaderless interval: leadership state is sampled at the end of the 1500ms observation window, so this probe does not measure an interval.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts. Three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming them as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The target is then chosen by configuration role, never by a measured result: in the control case the first voter that is not the leader, in the probe case the joined non-voter; its suffrage is read back from the leader's latest configuration and reported in the setup event. The case calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.id, target.addr), waits up to 5s for the returned result, then waits up to 1500ms for the requested target to be observed as Leader and separately for any node to be Leader, and finally records the leader set, the maximum term across all four nodes and whether that term rose above the leader's term before the call. Both cases share the harness TestAssuranceLeadershipTransferTarget and are emitted under distinct case names.

scope.description: Observe both halves of a leadership transfer request naming a non-voter: what LeadershipTransferToServer reports, which server actually holds leadership, and how the cluster's leadership state evolves during the attempt, sampled every millisecond, with the same call naming a voter as the control. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event and an assurance_transfer_result event carrying the returned result, the target and previous-leader states, leader sets and terms, and the sampling counters.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate, and protocol version >= 3 supports LeadershipTransferToServer.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a completed transfer.

Sampling every millisecond is fine-grained relative to the 200ms election timeout, so a leaderless interval lasting an election round is expected to be visible; shorter gaps are not bounded by this sampling rate.

experiments.revision_reason: The previous run of this harness answered the reported-result half of the question but sampled leadership state only at endpoints, so it could not say whether the cluster was ever without a leader or for how long. This revision adds a 1ms sampling goroutine running from the transfer call until after the observation window, reporting leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state, and the endpoint leader identity, with two comparisons asserting those observations for the non-voter case. Measured result fields, cases and target selection are unchanged.

scope.description: Run eight independent trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, arm a 600ms stall in the leader's log store, partition the leader so that only the non-voter remains reachable, drive a client Apply to block the leader's main loop on that store, queue VerifyLeader during the stall, and report the verify endpoint together with a 1ms leadership sampler over all four servers.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stalls; StoreLogs then blocks the leader's main loop, which is the goroutine that also serves the lease case and verify requests. The store is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; the stall is 600ms, three times the lease.
Only the elected leader's store is armed, so follower writes and their election timers behave as they would without the stall.
In-memory transports are used in one process, so RPC round trips are much faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: A leader blocked inside its own lease check rather than inside a store write, and host-level suspensions or clock jumps, which this probe does not reproduce.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store that wraps InmemStore and sleeps for 600ms inside StoreLogs while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster as Voter and the fourth node joins through the leader's own AddNonvoter call, with the trial waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The trial then emits assurance_stall_setup, disconnects the transports in both directions across the partition so that only the leader and the non-voter remain mutually reachable, starts a 1ms sampler that records every server's Leader state and the maximum term, arms the leader's stall, drives one Apply to make the leader write, queues VerifyLeader 300ms later, and reports assurance_stall_trial with the verify endpoint, the sample counters, the term reached, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyLeaderDuringLeaderStall.

comparisons.description: The stall was exercised and a different server was observed in Leader state at some point during or after it. Holds means the intended condition was reached.
Conditional on a successor having been observed: whether the queued VerifyLeader still reported success. Holds means the stale-read precondition was witnessed.
Restricted to trials where the stalled leader was never sampled outside Leader state: whether VerifyLeader reported success.

scope.description: Issue 64 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls in parallel against a freshly started single-voter node while Shutdown runs concurrently, count how many of those futures have not completed 400ms after Shutdown has returned, and compare with the same call kinds issued on a node that is never shut down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histogram and the shutdown error.
assumptions: A single-voter node is a supported configuration and makes each call complete quickly when the node is running, so any incomplete future is attributable to the shutdown race rather than to slow commit.
64 concurrent calls per trial is a probe of exposure, not a rate estimate; the concurrency is what makes the race observable.
Waiting 400ms after Shutdown() has returned is enough for any future that can still be answered, because the run loop has already exited by then.

Reconnecting the non-voter is a legal topology change: the transport is simply reconnected to a server that remains in the leader's latest configuration as a non-voter.

HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and a 900ms stall mean the leader's lease case cannot run during the stall while a voter majority can campaign at 200ms and elect a successor.
In-memory transports in one process, so RPC round trips are far faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: Multi-host clocks and process-level suspensions; and any case where the leader's own term is raised, since the partition keeps it at its old term.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.

Each server will track two configurations:
 1. its *committed configuration*: the latest configuration in the log/snapshot that has been committed, along with its index.
 2. its *latest configuration*: the latest configuration in the log/snapshot (may be committed or uncommitted), along with its index.

When there's no membership change happening, these two will be the same. The latest configuration is almost always the one used, except:
 - When followers truncate the suffix of their logs, they may need to fall back to the committed configuration.
 - When snapshotting, the committed configuration is written, to correspond with the committed log prefix that is being snapshotted.


## Application API

We propose the following operations for clients to manipulate the cluster configuration:
 - AddVoter: server becomes staging unless voter,
 - AddNonvoter: server becomes nonvoter unless staging or voter,
 - DemoteVoter: server becomes nonvoter unless absent,
 - RemovePeer: server removed from configuration,

result.summary: Opened a new sourced question about a public interface promise and requested its execution. ConfigurationStore documents StoreConfiguration as invoked once a committed configuration change exists, while BatchingFSM documents that ApplyBatch receives LogConfiguration entries; runFSM picks one path per FSM — applySingle calls StoreConfiguration, and applyBatch never does — so an FSM implementing both interfaces should see configuration changes only through ApplyBatch. The four source ranges for those interfaces and both apply paths were recorded, and the probe builds two three-voter clusters with the repository's own helper, triggers one configuration change by moving an existing voter's address, and reports the callback counts with controls for each interface. A construction run showed the shape of the answer — the ConfigurationStore-only FSM recorded 6 StoreConfiguration calls and no ApplyBatch config entries, while the FSM implementing both recorded 0 StoreConfiguration calls and 6 ApplyBatch config entries — but the retained execution decides the question and nothing is claimed from the construction run. Remaining work: interpreting that receipt and deciding whether the consequence (an application relying on StoreConfiguration to keep its durable FSM state complete receives nothing) is a defect under stated conditions or a documentation inconsistency to record as a negative result.

investigations.question: When the leader of a cluster that includes a non-voter can reach only that non-voter, does VerifyLeader's success still establish the voter-majority contact its stale-read protection is meant to provide?
investigations.hypothesis: VerifyLeader returns nil in that partition because the non-voter's AppendEntries acknowledgement is counted as a vote toward a quorum sized only over voters: quorumSize() counts voters in the latest configuration, while verifyFuture.vote increments on any notifyAll(true) arriving from any replication peer. Without any reachable peer the same call does not succeed, so the acknowledging non-voter is what satisfies the quorum.
investigations.discriminator: The returned endpoint of VerifyLeader at a leader partitioned so that (a) only the non-voter is reachable, (b) one voter is reachable, and (c) no peer is reachable, together with the quorum size and the suffrage of each server in the leader's latest configuration.

gaps.question: Which legal condition, if any, lets a successor be elected while the old leader still reports VerifyLeader success, given that the leader lease counts voters only and ReloadConfig cannot raise LeaderLeaseTimeout above HeartbeatTimeout?

investigations.question: When LeadershipTransferToServer names a non-voter, does the call report a transfer that the named server can actually complete, and what happens to the cluster's leadership while it cannot?
investigations.hypothesis: The leader does not check that the requested target holds a vote. It resolves the target through leaderState.replState, which holds an entry for every configured server except the leader itself, so a non-voter passes that check and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow makes it a candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer set, which skips pre-vote by design, so it sends a real RequestVote with a higher term. Each voter adopts that higher term and steps down before reaching the hasVote rejection, then refuses the vote because the candidate has no vote, so no server grants the transfer, yet the leader's transfer goroutine reports success when it observes its own leadership loss. The prediction is that the call returns nil while the requested target never becomes leader, whereas the same call naming a voter does transfer leadership.
investigations.discriminator: The transfer future's reported result compared with the state of the requested target and of the cluster's leadership, in two cases that differ only in the target's suffrage in the leader's latest configuration.

gaps.question: After a transfer request naming a non-voter, how long is the cluster without a leader, and does the previous leader lose leadership and the higher term before a new election completes?

investigations.question: When a leader's main loop is stalled past its lease while a voter majority elects a successor, can a VerifyLeader request queued during the stall still report success by counting the reachable non-voter's acknowledgement?
investigations.hypothesis: During the stall the leader keeps Leader state and its replication goroutines keep running, so a successor can be elected while the old leader still believes itself leader. The queued VerifyLeader cannot be served while the main loop is blocked; once the stall ends both the lease case and the verify case are ready, so the verify either registers and is answered nil after the non-voter's acknowledgement arrives, or the lease case is served first and the request is answered with leadership loss.
investigations.discriminator: The VerifyLeader endpoint of each trial alongside whether a different server was observed in Leader state while the stalled leader was still Leader, and the terms those servers held.

investigations.question: Can a future returned by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown is in progress be left permanently uncompleted, so that the caller's Error() never returns?
investigations.hypothesis: Each call creates a future whose send races the shutdown channel in one select. The channels are buffered (64 for verifyCh), so the send is ready immediately; when Shutdown closes shutdownCh the run loop may take the shutdown case with futures still queued, and because none of these futures sets ShutdownCh, deferError.Error() has nothing to unblock on. VerifyLeader should be the most exposed because the leader loop drains verifyCh one case per iteration, while applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries per iteration and Barrier shares that path.
investigations.discriminator: The number of futures per API call kind that have not completed 400ms after Shutdown() has returned, compared with the same call kinds on a node that is not shut down.

investigations.question: Can a follower hold a committed configuration that was never committed and then truncate its log so that its latest configuration names a server with no configuration entry behind it, and what does it do with that configuration?
investigations.hypothesis: processConfigurationLogEntry advances the committed configuration to the previous latest configuration whenever it installs a new one, without checking that the previous one was actually committed, and the appendEntries truncation path resets the latest configuration to the committed one when the conflicting suffix reaches past latestIndex. If a follower appends a configuration entry the leader never commits and later truncates that entry away, its latest configuration can still name the servers from that entry.
investigations.discriminator: A trace or probe that appends a configuration entry at a follower, leaves the leader's commit index below it, then forces the follower to truncate that index and compares the follower's latest configuration with the entries actually present in its log, together with what the follower then uses that configuration for (vote granting, election participation, lease counting).

investigations.question: When an application FSM implements both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore, is StoreConfiguration invoked for a committed configuration change as its documentation states, or is the change delivered only through ApplyBatch?
investigations.hypothesis: runFSM's applySingle calls StoreConfiguration for LogConfiguration entries only when the FSM is not a BatchingFSM, because applyBatch takes over entirely once batchingEnabled is true and handles configuration entries by sending them to ApplyBatch; the batching path contains no StoreConfiguration call, so the promise is not kept for an FSM that implements both interfaces.
investigations.discriminator: The callback counts of an FSM implementing both interfaces compared with an FSM implementing only ConfigurationStore, after one configuration change is committed through the leader.

scope.description: Issue 64 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls in parallel against a freshly started single-voter node while Shutdown runs concurrently, count how many of those futures have not completed 400ms after Shutdown has returned, and compare with the same call kinds issued on a node that is never shut down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histogram and the shutdown error.
assumptions: A single-voter node is a supported configuration and makes each call complete quickly when the node is running, so any incomplete future is attributable to the shutdown race rather than to slow commit.
64 concurrent calls per trial is a probe of exposure, not a rate estimate; the concurrency is what makes the race observable.
Waiting 400ms after Shutdown() has returned is enough for any future that can still be answered, because the run loop has already exited by then.

basis.prefix: Each case starts one real Raft instance in this process with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, bootstrapped as a single Voter with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms, and waits until it reports Leader. scope.description: Six trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, register a VerifyLeader request at the leader while it is isolated from every peer, stall its main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms, then reconnect only the non-voter after 250 to 500ms and record the verify endpoint, when a different server was first sampled in Leader state, whether that preceded the verdict, the terms involved and the stall counters.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stall blocks its own main loop; it is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
Reconnecting the non-voter is a legal topology change: the transport is simply reconnected to a server that remains in the leader's latest configuration as a non-voter.

HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and a 900ms stall mean the leader's lease case cannot run during the stall while a voter majority can campaign at 200ms and elect a successor.
In-memory transports in one process, so RPC round trips are far faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: Multi-host clocks and process-level suspensions; and any case where the leader's own term is raised, since the partition keeps it at its old term.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process with their own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store whose StoreLogs sleeps 900ms while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The three voters are bootstrapped as Voter and the fourth node joins through the leader's AddNonvoter call. The trial emits assurance_registered_setup, disconnects the leader from both other voters and from the non-voter, calls VerifyLeader on the leader, waits 30ms so the main loop registers the request, arms the stall and drives one Apply so the leader's main loop blocks inside StoreLogs, starts a 1ms sampler over all four servers, then after the configured delay reconnects only the leader and the non-voter and waits for the verify future. It emits assurance_registered_result with the endpoint, the verdict time, whether another server was sampled in Leader state and when, the maximum term seen, the leader's term and state, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyRegisteredThenStalled.

scope.description: Two cases, each a three-voter cluster built with the repository's own cluster helper whose FSMs share a recorder: one case where the FSM implements FSM and ConfigurationStore, and one where it also implements BatchingFSM. Each case triggers a single configuration change by moving an existing voter's address, waits until the change reaches the FSM, and reports how many times StoreConfiguration and ApplyBatch were called with configuration entries.
assumptions: Moving an existing voter's address is a legal configuration change that nextConfiguration accepts for a voter, and with three voters the entry commits on the leader and one other node before the moved address matters.
The recorder is shared across the cluster's FSMs only to answer whether the callback is ever invoked anywhere in the cluster; per-node attribution is not needed for that question.
The cluster helper builds in-memory transports and stores, so no external service is involved.
excluded: Whether an application should rely on StoreConfiguration when it also batches, and any behaviour of ApplyBatch ordering or responses.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.

Each server will track two configurations:
 1. its *committed configuration*: the latest configuration in the log/snapshot that has been committed, along with its index.
 2. its *latest configuration*: the latest configuration in the log/snapshot (may be committed or uncommitted), along with its index.

When there's no membership change happening, these two will be the same. The latest configuration is almost always the one used, except:
 - When followers truncate the suffix of their logs, they may need to fall back to the committed configuration.
 - When snapshotting, the committed configuration is written, to correspond with the committed log prefix that is being snapshotted.


## Application API

We propose the following operations for clients to manipulate the cluster configuration:
 - AddVoter: server becomes staging unless voter,
 - AddNonvoter: server becomes nonvoter unless staging or voter,
 - DemoteVoter: server becomes nonvoter unless absent,
 - RemovePeer: server removed from configuration,
